posts.quote: A BASEBALL CARD AND A CLOTHESPIN TURNED ANY BICYCLE INTO A MOTORCYCLE.
posts.caption: Every kid on the block knew the trick. You swiped one of Mom's wooden clothespins off the line and clipped a baseball card to the fork so it slapped against the spokes. The faster you pedaled, the louder it roared. Three or four of us would tear down the street sounding like a motorcycle gang, which, in our minds, we were. Nobody stopped to think about whose card it was. Somewhere out there is a grown man who flapped a fortune to shreds on a Schwinn and still doesn't want to talk about it.
posts.first:
I used my brother's doubles, which is the only reason I lived to be eleven. Mom never could figure out where all her clothespins went. Every one of them was on a bike somewhere in our neighborhood.

posts.quote: SUNDAY AFTERNOON, A FULL TANK, AND NOWHERE IN PARTICULAR TO GO.
posts.caption: After church and a big dinner, Dad would jingle the keys and say, let's go for a drive. That was the whole plan. No destination, no map, just back roads and the windows rolled down. We'd pass farms and little towns and maybe stop for a cone if he was in a good mood. Mom pointed out every house she'd like to live in. We kids fought over who got a window. You came home tired and sunburned on one arm, and somehow it felt like you'd been on vacation.
posts.first:
My dad called it 'burning a little gas,' and he said it like it was medicine. We'd usually end up at a fruit stand two counties over. I think now he just wanted a couple of quiet hours with all of us in one place.

posts.quote: NO SMUDGE ON EARTH COULD SURVIVE MOM'S HANDKERCHIEF AND A LITTLE SPIT.
posts.caption: You'd be standing on the church steps in your Sunday best, feeling pretty sharp. Then Mom would stop, squint, and reach into her purse. Out came the handkerchief. One quick lick, and before you could duck, she was scrubbing your cheek like she was trying to take the paint off a fence. You squirmed, you protested, you lost. And the worst part was, she was always right. There was something on your face.
posts.first:
My mother could find a smudge from across a parking lot. She'd have that handkerchief out before the car was in park. To this day I check my face in the rearview mirror before I walk into church.

posts.quote: DIAGRAMMING SENTENCES / WE TOOK EVERY SENTENCE APART ON THE CHALKBOARD AND PUT IT BACK TOGETHER
posts.caption: The teacher would write a sentence across the top of the chalkboard and call you up front. You drew the long line, split off the subject and the verb, and hung the adjectives underneath like laundry. A prepositional phrase meant another slanted line, and a compound sentence meant you'd be up there a while. The whole class watched while you worked it out, chalk dust all over your sleeve. Half of us hated it. The other half secretly loved it. Either way, every one of us still knows a dangling modifier when we see one.
posts.first:
I was terrible at it until a teacher told me to think of it like taking apart a lawn mower. After that it clicked. I still catch myself diagramming the sentences in the newspaper when I can't sleep.

posts.quote: Our street had one ladder, one set of jumper cables, and one tall man. Everybody borrowed all three.
posts.first:
The tall man on our street was Mr. Hollis, and he must have changed every high light bulb within four blocks. He never once said no. He'd just walk over in his slippers, reach up, and walk home.

posts.quote: MOM SPRINKLED THE SHIRTS, ROLLED THEM UP, AND IRONED ALL DAY TUESDAY.
posts.caption: Monday was wash day, so Tuesday was ironing day, and that was that. Mom filled an old soda bottle with water, jammed a sprinkler cap in the top, and dampened every shirt and pillowcase in the basket. Then she rolled them up tight and stacked them like loaves of bread. The board came out in the kitchen, the radio went on, and she worked through that pile until supper. The whole house smelled like hot cotton and starch. Dad never left for work in a wrinkled shirt, and none of us ever thought about why.
posts.first:
My mother even ironed the dish towels, and I teased her about it for years. Then I got married and bought my own iron. I don't iron dish towels, but I understand now why she did.

posts.quote: EVERY TOWN HAD A STORE WITH A POTBELLY STOVE AND THREE OLD MEN WHO NEVER BOUGHT ANYTHING.
posts.caption: You'd go in for a box of nails or a loaf of bread and find the same three men around the stove. They'd been there since breakfast. One of them had a checkerboard on a pickle barrel, one had opinions about the weather, and one just whittled. They never seemed to buy a thing, and the owner never seemed to mind. They were the town's newspaper, weather bureau, and city council all in one. If you wanted to know what was going on, you just stood near the stove and warmed your hands.
posts.first:
Our store had a bench right by the stove that my grandpa claimed was his. I sat on it once when I was about eight and three grown men stopped talking. I never sat on it again.

posts.character: Humor about today vs. then (Grandpa's knee)
posts.quote: WE DIDN'T NEED A WEATHER REPORT. WE HAD GRANDPA'S KNEE.
posts.caption: Grandpa would be sitting on the porch, perfectly fine, and then he'd rub his knee and squint at the sky. 'Rain by suppertime,' he'd say. The radio said clear skies all day. Grandma would sigh and go take the sheets off the line anyway. Sure enough, around five, the first drops would hit the porch roof. Nobody ever argued with that knee. It had more years of experience than the weatherman, and it was right more often.
posts.first:
My grandfather blamed his knee on a fall off a hay wagon in 1931. He used it to call every storm for forty years. When I started getting a twinge before the rain myself, I called my mother and told her I'd inherited the family forecast.

posts.quote: THE ENCYCLOPEDIA SALESMAN / TWENTY-SIX VOLUMES, A DOLLAR DOWN, AND A BOOKSHELF THAT WEIGHED MORE THAN THE COUCH
posts.caption: He showed up on a weeknight in a pressed suit with a sample case that must have weighed forty pounds. Mom let him in because he was polite and it was cold out. He sat on the edge of the couch and opened that case like it held the crown jewels. By the end of the evening he'd convinced Dad that no child could get through school without a full set. A few weeks later, twenty-six books arrived in a heavy box. We used them for every report until high school, and they were still on that shelf the day the house sold.
posts.first:
We bought ours a dollar a week for what felt like the rest of my childhood. I read the whole 'S' volume one summer because I was stuck inside with the measles. I still know more about Saturn than anybody should.

posts.quote: YOU SAID 'YES, SIR' AND 'NO, MA'AM,' AND YOU MEANT EVERY WORD.
posts.caption: It didn't matter if it was the mailman, the principal, or the lady from down the street. If a grown-up spoke to you, the answer started with yes, sir or no, ma'am. Forget it once and you'd hear about it before you got home, because news traveled faster than kids did. It wasn't about being afraid. It was about knowing that other people mattered too. Somewhere along the way it stuck, and plenty of us still can't answer a question without it.
posts.first:
I said 'yes, ma'am' to a woman about my own age at the grocery store last year, and she laughed and asked where I grew up. I told her a little town where you didn't have a choice. She said, 'Me too,' and we stood there grinning like a couple of kids.
